1: Open with a question: “When did a customer or candidate last chase you for an update?” Every time that happens, we’ve already lost a bit of control. This session sets one standard: nobody waits on us, nothing is held back, and both sides are coached through every step. It builds on Module 07 (Client Control) and Module 08 (Interview Prep).
2: Ask everyone to have one live role open with its candidates; you’ll use it in the exercise.
3: When a customer or candidate hears nothing, they fill the gap with the worst assumption: the agency isn’t working on it, the candidate has gone cold, the role has gone away. A candidate who hears nothing for a week takes another interview. A customer who hears nothing calls another agency. Over-communicating feels like too much to us; to the other side it feels like being looked after. Five minutes.
4: Ask the room to be honest: which of the “stop” column do you do? Most people recognise the first two. Holding information usually comes from a good place, such as not wanting to bother anyone or waiting until there’s an answer, but it reads as silence. “No news” is still news: it tells the other side you’re on it and when they’ll hear next. Eight minutes.
5: This is the minimum standard. The 48-hour rule is the one that changes behaviour most: while anything is waiting, both sides hear from you at least every 48 hours, even if the update is “still waiting, here’s what I’m doing about it”. Tell the customer and candidate this cadence at the start so they know what to expect. That alone cuts down on chasing. Ask people to screenshot or print this slide for their desk. Ten minutes.
6: Ask each customer and candidate early how they prefer to be updated, and use it: many hiring managers now want a shared Slack channel; many candidates prefer text. Whatever the channel, the call-then-confirm rule applies to anything important, so there’s always a written record. Keep messages short. A three-line Slack update read today beats a long email read next week. Five minutes.
7: Every customer message should end with a clear ask and a date: that’s how you coach the customer and keep control (Module 07). The recap email puts the agreed process in writing on day one and sets the update rhythm, so the customer never wonders when they’ll hear from you. Have everyone draft a Slack update for their live role now; three minutes.
8: Candidate control comes from coaching, not chasing. A candidate who knows exactly what happens next, and when they’ll hear from you, doesn’t go quiet or take another process without telling you. Each step links back to a module: prep and pre-close (Module 08), counteroffer and resignation (Module 09). The tip is the core habit: end every candidate conversation with the next step, the date and when you’ll next speak. Five minutes.
9: The “no news yet” message is the one most consultants never send, and it’s the one that keeps candidates warm. Notice it does three things: it gives the status, it pre-closes (“still a 9/10?”) and it commits to a specific next contact. Have everyone write one for a candidate in their live process and send it before the end of the session. Five minutes.
10: The instinct is to hold bad news until we’ve fixed it. Don’t. A customer who finds out late loses trust; a customer who hears it early, with a plan, trusts you more. The same applies to candidates: a rejection delivered quickly, by phone, with honest feedback keeps them in your network for the next role. Pairs practise delivering one piece of bad news each, five minutes.
11: Run this check in the last 15 minutes of every day. The last item is the real test: if you were off sick tomorrow, could someone on the team pick up every live deal from your CRM notes? If not, there’s information in your head that should be written down. Managers can spot-check two live deals per consultant each week against this list.
12: Use real roles so the messages go out today. In the review, partners look for three things: anyone left waiting over 48 hours, any message without a clear next step and date, and anything important being sent by text that should be a call. Finish by having everyone send their two messages before leaving the room.
13: Ask each person which habit from the “stop” list they’re dropping first. Managers: in the weekly pipeline review, ask “when did the customer and candidate last hear from you?” for every live deal. If the answer is more than 48 hours, that deal is at risk.
14: Open the floor for questions. Close by asking everyone to confirm they’ve sent their two messages from the exercise.
